prompt.context: A light bulb manufacturer currently sells light bulbs for $1 that last one year and cost $0.50 to produce. There are three other competitors, and each of the four producers has 25% market share. The company has developed a new light bulb that lasts 10 years and costs $1 to produce.
prompt.question: You can produce either the old or the new bulb. Which one do you decide to sell?

framework: Analyze cost structure: company likely has low variable costs and high fixed costs, so volume is important
Price analysis: determine consumer indifference price between old and new bulb
Competitive dynamics: assess whether competitors will develop the new bulb and how quickly
Demand/volume impact: a 10-year bulb reduces replacement frequency — model revenue implications
Product positioning: evaluate whether the new bulb shifts the product from commodity to durable/appliance
Customer acquisition and conversion: consider how to pace customer adoption over the 10-year cycle

questions.prompt: At what price would a consumer be indifferent between the old bulb ($1, lasts 1 year) and the new bulb (lasts 10 years)?
questions.guidance: A consumer buying the old bulb spends $1/year, or $10 over 10 years. Therefore the new bulb should be priced at $10 to achieve consumer indifference. A lower price could attract volume and gain market share; a higher price risks rejection of an unproven product.

math.setup: Old bulb cost over 10 years = $1/year x 10 years. New bulb is bought once for 10 years.
steps: Consumer indifference price for new bulb = $10

questions.prompt: Compare profitability: old bulb vs. new bulb assuming consumer indifference pricing.
questions.guidance: Old bulb: revenue $1, cost $0.50, margin $0.50 per bulb. Over 10 years a customer buys 10 bulbs: total margin = $5. New bulb: revenue $10, cost $1, margin $9 per bulb (one sale per customer per 10 years). The new bulb yields significantly higher margin per customer over the same period, even though volume per customer drops 10x.

math.setup: Compare 10-year margin per customer for each product.
steps: Old bulb 10-year margin per customer = $0.50 x 10 = $5.00
New bulb 10-year margin per customer (1 unit) = $9.00
math.answer: New bulb generates $9 vs. $5 per customer over 10 years — 80% higher margin

questions.prompt: What competitive risks arise from launching the new bulb?
questions.guidance: If competitors develop the same new bulb and regain their 25% shares, the company may have invested in new production capacity that is no longer needed, leaving excess capacity. First-mover advantage may be temporary. The company should consider how long it takes competitors to replicate and price to build a loyal customer base quickly.

brainstorming.prompt: What strategic and operational issues should the company consider when deciding to launch and price the new long-life bulb?

categories.name: Pricing & Willingness to Pay
ideas: Price at consumer indifference point ($10) as baseline
Consider lower price to grow market share faster
Unproven product may face resistance at 10x price — warranties or guarantees could help

categories.name: Product Positioning
ideas: Shift framing from commodity to durable home appliance (like TVs, PCs, cars)
Market and distribute through appliance channels, not grocery/hardware commodity channels
Emphasize total cost of ownership rather than sticker price

categories.name: Competitive Dynamics
ideas: How long before competitors develop an equivalent new bulb?
First-mover advantage in brand trust and customer lock-in
Risk of excess capacity if competitors catch up and reclaim share
Consider IP/patent protection on the new bulb technology

categories.name: Customer Adoption & Revenue Smoothing
ideas: Bulb lasting 10 years eliminates replacement purchases — potential revenue cliff
Strategy to acquire customers in a way that spreads conversions evenly over time
Target new-home buyers, commercial/B2B customers, and renovators as recurring entry points
Subscription or guarantee programs to maintain customer relationship

categories.name: Cost & Operations
ideas: New bulb costs $1 vs $0.50 for old — variable cost doubles
Fixed cost base likely large; new bulb's higher margin helps absorb fixed costs
Production conversion: can the same facilities make both bulbs?

recommendation: Produce and sell the new long-life bulb
Price at or near the consumer indifference price of $10, with possible introductory pricing to accelerate adoption
Position as a durable home appliance, not a commodity
risks: Consumers may be unwilling to pay $10 upfront for an unproven product without a guarantee
Competitors may develop equivalent bulbs quickly, eliminating first-mover advantage and stranding capacity investments
10-year product life collapses replacement demand, requiring continuous new-customer acquisition to sustain revenues
next_steps: Assess consumer willingness to pay through market research; design warranty/guarantee to reduce perceived risk
Evaluate competitor R&D timelines and consider patent protection
Model customer acquisition curves to avoid a revenue cliff in years 7-10
Develop appliance-style go-to-market strategy (retail placement, packaging, messaging)
